books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, A. Religious and Spiritual Movements in Antebellum America

stimulus.text: In August 1801, the Presbyterian minister Barton W. Stone hosted a communion service at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, that became the largest camp meeting of the Great Revival in the West. For six days, from August 6 to 12, crowds estimated at ten to twenty thousand people gathered on the grounds, far more than the log meetinghouse, which seated about four hundred, could hold. Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers all preached, and hundreds took communion at tables set up in the woods.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Disciples of Christ Historical Society account of the Cane Ridge Revival and the National Park Service nomination for Cane Ridge: August 6-12, 1801; Barton W. Stone; estimates of ten to twenty thousand; meetinghouse capacity about four hundred; Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the Disciples Historical Society / NPS account of Cane Ridge (1801)
stem: The size of the crowd at Cane Ridge most directly shows which of the following about the early Second Great Awakening?

options.text: Revival religion drew crowds far beyond what any church could hold
Most Americans in 1801 belonged to the Presbyterian Church
options.misconception: Stone was a Presbyterian minister, so the crowd can look like a Presbyterian majority.

options.text: The federal government organized religious meetings on the frontier
options.misconception: The meeting was large and orderly, so it can look like a government-organized event.

options.text: Frontier settlers had largely abandoned religion before the revival began
options.misconception: The revival looks like a new beginning, so it can seem that nobody believed anything before it.

rationales.A: Ten to twenty thousand people came to a meetinghouse that seated four hundred. The crowd itself proves revival religion had outgrown the building.
rationales.B: Methodist and Baptist preachers also preached at Cane Ridge, and the crowd came from many churches. No single denomination held a majority.
rationales.C: Stone, a Presbyterian minister, organized the meeting with other preachers. The federal government had no part in it.
rationales.D: The crowds came because frontier religion was already alive: the meeting was a communion service, a tradition settlers already kept.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the two numbers: a meetinghouse for four hundred, and a crowd of ten to twenty thousand.
2. Ask what the gap means: the revival had outgrown the building, so it moved outdoors.
3. Name the pattern: mass religion, drawing crowds no church could contain.
Background: Cane Ridge was the largest camp meeting of the Great Revival in the West.
Remember: when the crowd outgrows the building, the building is no longer the story.
